title: Reproduce as the account that actually runs it
explanation: `sudo -u monitor /usr/local/bin/healthcheck` fails with `Permission denied`. Running it as root would fail identically here, which is itself a useful signal -- unlike ordinary DAC read/write checks, the execute bit is one permission root doesn't get to skip.

title: Check the mode
explanation: `ls -l /usr/local/bin/healthcheck` shows `-rw-r--r--` (644) -- read permission everywhere, but no `x` bit for anyone, owner included. A "config-management normalized modes" run is a classic way to end up here: something blindly set every file to a read/write default without checking whether it needed to stay executable.

title: Understand why this fails even for root
explanation: `execve()` refuses to run a file with no execute bit set, full stop -- this is one of the few DAC checks the kernel enforces regardless of caller privilege. That's different from a read/write permission problem, where root always has an escape hatch; here even root would hit the exact same `Permission denied` trying to exec this file directly.

title: Restore the execute bit
explanation: `sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/healthcheck` adds execute for owner, group, and other (mode becomes `755`), matching what a script meant to be run directly needs.

title: Verify as the real user
explanation: `sudo -u monitor /usr/local/bin/healthcheck` should now print `OK` -- confirming `monitor` can invoke it directly, the same way the monitoring agent does every minute.
